name: Buff Orange
lede: Buff Orange is a soft yellow-orange from the colour lists of the early nineteenth-century naturalists, matched to a kingfisher's eye-streak and the stamens of a white cistus flower.

sections.title: A kingfisher, a flower and a stone
sections.body:
In Patrick Syme's chart, Buff Orange is number 77, the second of the oranges [1]. His examples from nature are the streak beside the eye of the kingfisher, the stamens of the large white cistus, and a silicate mineral, natrolite [1]. The kingfisher is *Alcedo atthis*, and the cistus is a rockrose [2].

The recipe is sienna yellow with a little Dutch orange [2]. Dutch orange is the preceding colour on the chart, a mix of gamboge yellow and carmine red [2]. Syme's next orange is built from Buff Orange itself: Reddish Orange is Buff Orange with a considerable portion of tile red [3].

The screen swatch is warm and light, and our library finds [[tan]] its nearest common name [4]. It is not the buff of leather and army coats. That colour has its own article, [[buff]].

sections.title: In the lists
sections.body:
Buff Orange appears in Cleaveland's American mineralogy textbook of 1816, in a list of 80 colours adapted from Jameson, and in Syme's chart [5]. Syme's second edition of 1821 added only one blue and one red, so the orange was already in his first book of 1814 [6]. Baty's chart does not show it in Jameson's list of 1805, and the books consulted do not say who coined it [5].

Syme's chart was perhaps the only one used by English-speaking botanists until 1886 [7]. In a botanical list Baty reproduces, Buff Orange is the colour assigned to the common tulip [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a colour within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 493 works, or 2.1 per cent [8]. India has the most: 42 of 721 Indian works carry it, and 18 of the 168 Mughal paintings [8]. Japan follows with 33 of 698 [8].

Three of the four largest patches are Japanese: Reizei's *Twelve Poetic Immortals and Their Poems*, of 1845, where the match fills 82 per cent of the picture, then Kanō Tsunenobu's fan album of 1636 and Kishi Ganku's *Bamboo* of 1801 [8]. See [[painting:aic-198910|Bamboo]] for the quieter, paper-ground version. By decade it peaks in the 1820s, with 40 of 731 works [8]. Among painters with enough works to compare, Sir Henry Raeburn stands out, with 4 of 12 [8]. It sits with [[marigold]], [[mustard]] and [[ochre]] more than chance would predict [8]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so read them as screen colours, not pigment tests [8].
